The test fails because it builds the expected date with the local timezone, while the parser returns UTC. On your machine the two agree, since your clock is set to UTC, but the CI runner uses Europe/Berlin and shifts the value by two hours. That is why the assertion compares 14:00 against 12:00 and fails only in CI.

The fix is to construct the expected value with an explicit UTC zone, which makes the test independent of the runner settings. I changed that line and ran the suite twice with TZ set to Berlin, and both runs passed.

The test fails in CI. It builds the expected date in local time. The parser returns UTC. Your machine runs on UTC. The CI runner uses Europe/Berlin. That shifts the value by two hours. The assertion compares 14:00 with 12:00.

The fix uses an explicit UTC zone. The test no longer depends on the runner. I changed that line. I ran the suite twice with TZ set to Berlin. Both runs passed.

The cache sits in front of the product service and keeps each response in Redis for five minutes, keyed by product ID and locale. When a request comes in, the handler checks Redis first and only calls the service on a miss, after which it stores the fresh response with the same TTL.

Price updates do not wait for the TTL, because the admin panel publishes an invalidation event that deletes the matching keys. If Redis is unavailable, the handler falls back to the service directly, so a cache outage slows pages down but does not break them.

Migration 0042 adds a nullable `archived_at` column to the `projects` table and backfills it from the old `is_archived` flag, using the `updated_at` timestamp for rows that were already archived. It does not drop `is_archived` yet, because the reporting job still reads that column and would break on the next nightly run.

The backfill runs in batches of 5,000 rows, so it should not lock the table for long on production, where the table has about 1.2 million rows. Once the reporting job is updated, a second migration can remove the old flag.

`pool_size` sets how many database connections each worker keeps open, and the default of 10 is too high for your setup. You run 12 workers against a Postgres instance that allows 100 connections, so at peak the app asks for 120 and the last requests fail with "too many clients".

Setting it to 6 keeps the total at 72, which leaves room for migrations and the admin console. If requests start waiting on the pool, raise `max_connections` on the database instead of raising the pool, because the database is the shared limit.

The duplicate rows came from the pagination query, which computed the offset as `page * size` while the frontend counts pages from 1. Page 1 therefore skipped the first 20 items, and the last page repeated items that had already appeared, which is what users reported as duplicates.

I changed the query so it subtracts one from the page number before computing the offset, and I added a test that walks all pages of a 45-item list and checks that every ID appears exactly once. The API contract stays the same, so the mobile app needs no update.

The switch step is the last part of the deploy, and it only runs after the green environment has passed its health checks for five minutes. It updates the load balancer so that new requests go to green, while blue keeps serving the requests that are already in flight until they finish.

Blue stays up for an hour after the switch, because rolling back is then just a matter of pointing the load balancer at it again. After that hour the pipeline scales blue down to zero, which frees the nodes for the next release.

For this service I would pick httpx over requests, mainly because the new ingestion worker is async and httpx offers the same API in both sync and async form. Requests is more mature and has a larger ecosystem of adapters, but it blocks the event loop, so you would have to push every call into a thread pool.

Httpx also supports HTTP/2 and has stricter timeout defaults, which matters when the upstream API is slow. The migration is small, since most call sites only use `get` and `post` with JSON bodies.

The orders page is slow because the query filters by `customer_id` and sorts by `created_at`, but the table only has an index on `customer_id`. Postgres finds the customer rows quickly and then sorts about 80,000 of them in memory for every request, which accounts for most of the 1.4 seconds.

A composite index on `(customer_id, created_at DESC)` lets Postgres read the rows already in order and stop after the first 50. I tested it on a copy of production, where the query dropped to 12 milliseconds, and the index adds about 300 MB.

The CI job fails at the install step because `package-lock.json` no longer matches `package.json`. You added `zod` locally with a newer npm version, which rewrote the lockfile format, and the runner still uses npm 8, so `npm ci` refuses to install from a file it considers out of sync.

There are two ways out: regenerate the lockfile with npm 8, or bump the runner to Node 20, which ships npm 10. I would bump the runner, since the other workflows already use Node 20 and the team planned that upgrade anyway.

The 429 responses come from the partner API, which allows 100 requests per minute per key, and the import job sends up to 400 because it runs four workers that share one key. Each worker retries immediately after a 429, so a burst of failures makes the next minute even worse.

I added a shared token bucket in Redis that all workers draw from, and retries now wait for the time in the `Retry-After` header. With that change the import of 12,000 records took 2 hours instead of failing after 20 minutes.

The plan keeps nightly full backups of the Postgres database for 30 days and streams the write-ahead log to object storage every minute, so we can restore to any point in the last month with at most a minute of lost data. Backups go to a bucket in a second region, which protects them if the primary region goes down.

Once a month a scheduled job restores the latest backup into a staging instance and runs a row count check, because a backup that was never restored is only a guess.

The upload fails with EACCES because the app container runs as user `node`, while the `/data/uploads` volume was created by root when you first mounted it. The process can read the directory but cannot create files in it, which is why downloads work and uploads do not.

The cleanest fix is to set the owner of the volume to UID 1000 in the init container, so the permissions are correct on every fresh deploy. Running the app as root would also work, but it would give any exploit in the upload handler full access to the container.

The logs show that the checkout errors started at 09:14, right after the payment service deployed version 3.8, and they stop at 09:52 when it rolled back. Almost all of the 1,320 errors are timeouts on the `/authorize` call, which went from a median of 180 ms to over 5 seconds during that window.

The new version opened a fresh TLS connection for every request, so the connection pool never warmed up. Other services look normal, and the database latency stayed flat, which rules out a shared cause.

I went through the whole retry path, from the HTTP client through the queue consumer and into the dead-letter handler, and checked every place where an exception could be swallowed or turned into a silent success. There is exactly one. It sits in `ack_message`, which returns early when the payload is empty and never logs it, so those messages disappear without a trace. Adding a warning there and counting the cases in the metrics would close the gap.

Upgrading the ORM from 4.x to 5.x touched more files than I expected, because the new version changes how lazy relations are loaded and every serializer that walked a relation needed an explicit `select_related`. The tests pass. All of them. I also compared the query count on the five busiest endpoints before and after, and none of them got worse, while the order detail page dropped from 41 queries to 6.

The flaky test was not flaky in the sense people usually mean, since it failed every time the suite ran after the cache tests, which leave a global fixture behind. Order mattered. Once I reset the fixture in teardown, the test passed in 200 random orderings, and I removed the retry decorator that had been hiding the problem for months.

Changes in 1.9.2:

Fixed a crash when the config file is empty. Added Brazilian Portuguese translations. Dropped support for Python 3.8. Raised the default request timeout to 30 seconds. Renamed the `verbose` option to `log_level`. Thanks to the four new contributors who sent patches this cycle.

To rotate the API key without downtime:

1. Create a second key in the partner dashboard.
2. Add it to the secret store as `PARTNER_KEY_NEXT`.
3. Deploy the app, which accepts both keys.
4. Switch traffic to the new key.
5. Revoke the old key after 24 hours.

If anything fails before step 5, the old key still works, so you can stop and retry.

If the build cache is corrupted, reset it like this:

1. Stop the dev server.
2. Delete the `.turbo` and `node_modules/.cache` folders.
3. Run `pnpm install`.
4. Start the server again.

The first build afterwards takes about two minutes, because nothing is cached yet.

The memory growth comes from the thumbnail worker, which keeps a reference to every decoded image in a module-level dictionary that was meant as a cache but has no size limit. Over a day of normal traffic it reaches about 3 GB, and the OOM killer stops the container around 18:00 each evening. That matches the restarts. Replacing the dictionary with an LRU cache of 500 entries keeps memory under 400 MB in my load test, and the hit rate stays above 90 percent.

Feature flags in this project live in `flags.yaml`, and the loader reads the file once at startup, so a change needs a restart unless you use the admin endpoint, which reloads the file in place and logs the diff. Most teams prefer the endpoint. It is faster, and it leaves an audit trail that the restart path does not, which helped us last month when someone flipped a flag by mistake.

Die Wiederherstellung haben wir im September geprobt, wobei 2 TB in knapp vier Stunden zurückgespielt waren.

Der Notfallplan hat zwei Teile. Der S3-Bucket ist versioniert. Gelöschte Objekte bleiben 90 Tage wiederherstellbar. Dann kopiert ein Job jede Nacht alle Objekte. Sie landen in einem zweiten Konto. Das Produktivsystem darf dort nicht schreiben. Ein kompromittierter Schlüssel löscht also nichts.

Im September haben wir die Wiederherstellung geprobt. Es ging um 2 TB. Das dauerte knapp vier Stunden.

Jonas hat vorgeschlagen, die Datei zeilenweise zu streamen, und dafür auch gleich ein Beispiel verlinkt.

Die restlichen Kommentare betreffen Benennungen und zwei fehlende Tests, die du auch in einem eigenen PR nachreichen kannst.

Die alten Produktbilder tauchen noch auf, weil das CDN sie 30 Tage lang zwischenspeichert und unsere Bilder bei einer Änderung denselben Dateinamen behalten. Ein manuelles Purge hilft zwar kurzfristig, aber Browser, die das Bild schon geladen haben, fragen das CDN gar nicht erst wieder an.

Am saubersten ist es, einen Hash des Inhalts in den Dateinamen aufzunehmen, sodass jede neue Version eine neue URL bekommt. Die lange Cache-Dauer kann dann bleiben, und wir sparen weiterhin den Großteil des Traffics.

Ich habe die gesamte Kette vom Upload über die Virenprüfung bis zur Ablage im Archiv durchgesehen und jede Stelle geprüft, an der eine Datei verloren gehen oder doppelt gespeichert werden könnte. Es gibt genau eine. Sie liegt in `move_to_archive`, das bei einem Netzwerkfehler die Quelldatei schon gelöscht hat, bevor die Kopie bestätigt ist. Wenn wir die Reihenfolge umdrehen, ist das Risiko weg.

Nach dem Upgrade auf PHP 8.3 mussten wir an überraschend vielen Stellen nachbessern, weil dynamische Properties jetzt eine Warnung auslösen und unser Logging jede Warnung als Fehler behandelt. Die Tests sind grün. Alle 1.214. Auch die Antwortzeiten der zehn meistgenutzten Endpunkte haben wir vorher und nachher gemessen, und keiner ist langsamer geworden.

Der Fehler trat nur auf, wenn zwei Nutzer dieselbe Bestellung innerhalb weniger Millisekunden bearbeiteten, was im Alltag selten vorkommt und sich deshalb lange versteckt hat. Dann aber zuverlässig. Mit einer Versionsspalte und optimistischem Locking bekommt der zweite Schreibvorgang jetzt eine klare Meldung, statt die Änderungen des ersten still zu überschreiben.

Stand der Migration heute Abend:

- Datenbank: auf Postgres 16 umgezogen.
- Mailversand: läuft über den neuen Anbieter.
- Alte Server: noch bis Freitag erreichbar.
- DNS: TTL auf fünf Minuten gesenkt.
- Offen: das Zertifikat für die Staging-Domain.

Das Zertifikat beantrage ich morgen früh, die übrigen Punkte brauchen keine weitere Arbeit.

Kurzer Überblick über den Testserver. Die Platte ist zu 64 Prozent belegt. Das letzte Sicherheitsupdate lief am Montag. Nginx läuft in Version 1.26. Drei Cronjobs sind deaktiviert.

Nichts davon blockiert den Release, aber die deaktivierten Cronjobs sollten wir vor dem Audit noch prüfen.

Änderungen in Version 4.2.1:

Der Absturz beim Öffnen leerer Projekte ist behoben. Die Oberfläche gibt es jetzt auch auf Polnisch. Die Unterstützung für Windows 8 entfällt. Das Standardlimit für Uploads liegt nun bei 50 MB. Die Option `debug` heißt jetzt `log_level`. Danke an alle, die in diesem Zyklus Fehler gemeldet haben.

So setzt du die lokale Datenbank zurück:

1. Stoppe alle Container.
2. Lösche das Volume `pgdata`.
3. Starte die Container neu.
4. Führe `make seed` aus.

Danach hast du wieder die Testdaten vom Stand des letzten Releases. Eigene Testkonten musst du neu anlegen, weil das Löschen des Volumes alles entfernt.

Für den neuen API-Schlüssel gehst du so vor:

1. Melde dich im Partnerportal an.
2. Erzeuge unter „Zugänge“ einen neuen Schlüssel.
3. Trage ihn im Tresor als `PARTNER_KEY` ein.
4. Starte den Import-Dienst neu.
5. Lösche den alten Schlüssel im Portal.

Bis Schritt 5 funktioniert der alte Schlüssel weiter, falls etwas schiefgeht.

Der Speicherverbrauch steigt, weil der PDF-Generator für jede Rechnung eine neue Browser-Instanz startet und diese bei einem Fehler im Template nicht wieder schließt, sodass im Laufe eines Tages Dutzende verwaiste Chromium-Prozesse übrig bleiben. Das erklärt die Neustarts. Mit einem `finally`-Block, der den Browser in jedem Fall schließt, blieb der Speicher im Lasttest über acht Stunden stabil bei etwa 600 MB.

Die Feature-Flags liegen in der Tabelle `flags` und werden beim Start in den Speicher geladen, weshalb eine Änderung erst nach einem Neustart greift, es sei denn, man nutzt den Admin-Endpunkt, der die Tabelle neu einliest und die Änderung protokolliert. Die meisten Teams nehmen den Endpunkt. Er ist schneller, und das Protokoll hat uns im Sommer geholfen, als jemand ein Flag versehentlich umgeschaltet hat.
